title: Police Vehicles, Emergency Response & Rideshare
citation: NJTR-1 Crash Report Manual (2023), Appendix: General Questions
key_points: Responding to Emergency ends once the patrol car is positioned at the scene.
A no-lights, no-siren response to a real emergency still counts as responding; explain in the narrative.
Uber or Lyft drivers count as Business/Commerce only while carrying a passenger or on the way to pick one up.

faq.q: My patrol car is parked at a crash scene and gets hit. Do I check Responding to Emergency?
faq.a: No. Once the car is positioned at the scene, the emergency response is over.

faq.q: I was answering an emergency call with no lights or siren (tactical approach) and crashed.
faq.a: Still check Responding to Emergency, and explain the reason for the silent response in the narrative.

faq.q: Is a rideshare driver personal use or business?
faq.a: Mark vehicle use 02 – Business/Commerce only if they were carrying a passenger or driving to pick one up for hire. Otherwise it's personal use.

faq.q: Is there insurance coverage when I crash a patrol car?
faq.a: Generally your municipality's insurance carrier covers it.

faq.q: Is a police car stopped in the road at a crash or traffic stop "in transport"?
faq.a: Yes, whether or not its emergency lights are on. A patrol car on patrol or responding to a call is also in transport.
